definition: Marginalization means the process of pushing a person or group to the edges of society, where they are treated as unimportant and denied real influence.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word marginalization. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know marginalization should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Historians traced the marginalization of the immigrant dockworkers, who were barred from union meetings and passed over for every promotion.
An oversight is weaker — it is a one-time accidental overlooking of someone, without marginalization's sense of an ongoing pattern that pushes people to the edge.
Ostracism is stronger — it is total, deliberate banishment from the group, going beyond marginalization's edge-of-the-room treatment to complete exclusion.

Exclusion is the act of shutting someone out of a group or activity — a locked door, a name left off a list — and it can happen a single time. Marginalization is slower and more corrosive: people are let into the room but pushed to its edges, treated as unimportant and denied real influence, again and again.

Sidelining is the everyday word for pushing someone out of the action or out of decisions — benched, ignored, talked over. Marginalization names the same pushing-aside as an ongoing social process, in the formal register of essays and reports. A teammate gets sidelined; a community gets marginalized in a policy study.

Disempowerment is the stripping away of a person's or group's power or influence — the levers are taken out of their hands. Marginalization is about position as much as power: people are shoved to society's edges and treated as not mattering. Disempowerment removes control; marginalization removes standing and voice.

For most of the last century, the deaf residents of Harwick experienced a quiet marginalization that no law ever spelled out.
They were never barred from town meetings; the doors stood open, and their names appeared on the voter rolls like everyone else's.
But no interpreter was ever hired, their petitions were filed at the bottom of every agenda, and officials treated the deaf community as not worth planning for.
Decade after decade, the pattern repeated: present in the room, absent from every decision that mattered.
Only in the 1990s, when a new council seated deaf advisers and funded interpreters, did residents say the town finally treated them as people whose voices counted.
